title: Met Office shares how to see the Northern Lights from the UK tonight
excerpt: Don't worry if you missed out on this weekend's spectacle
content:
Don't worry if you missed out on this weekend's spectacle

16:57, 11 Oct 2026Updated 16:58, 11 Oct 2026

Stargazers were treated to a dazzling Northern Lights display which was visible across large parts of the UK last night. The Met Office said they may be visible again in the coming nights.

‌

‌

The aurora borealis, commonly known as the Northern Lights, lit up skies over northern England in the early hours of today, Sunday (October 11). Stunning photos also captured the green and pink spectacle as far south as Kent and Surrey.

‌

But those who missed out could be lucky enough to catch a glimpse of the Northern Lights from the UK again on Sunday and Monday night.

‌

When you can see the Northern Lights

Met Office forecaster Greg Dewhurst said: “They could be a little weaker tonight (Sunday), so most likely seen across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England. They may be a little stronger again on Monday night so could be seen further south into central areas.”

The spectacle can sometimes be better seen through a camera than by the naked eye. Mr Dewhurst said: “Long exposure camera shots may show something each night a little further south than the above visible by eye forecast."

‌

The phenomenon is most visible in the time around the equinoxes in spring and autumn. It is triggered by solar activity, the Met Office said.

The sun emits charged particles known as solar wind, which, when they interact with the Earth’s magnetic field, are funnelled towards the magnetic poles. As the energetic particles collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, they release energy as light.

‌

Oxygen produces a green colour and, at higher altitudes, red, while nitrogen creates blue and purple hues, the weather forecaster said.

The autumn equinox in the Northern Hemisphere occurred on Wednesday, September 23, 2026, at 01.05 BST in the UK, as tracked by the Royal Museums Greenwich. The Sun crossed directly above the Earth's equator, which marks the start of astronomical autumn.

How to see the Northern Lights from the UK

The sky needs to be as clear as possible, and they are often picked up better through a camera on your phone. This is because cameras on devices are able to view more light than the human eye.

‌

It is best to wait until after 9pm when it is dark, and you should face northwards for the best chance of catching a glimpse. Rural locations are often better than cities and towns as pollution from artificial lights can make it more difficult to see the colourful display.
